question: A manager has fifteen minutes to check a six-page recommendation before a decision meeting. She cannot verify everything in it. What should she concentrate on?
options: A) The passages that are written most confidently, because strongly worded claims carry the most weight in a meeting.
B) An even sample drawn from each of the six pages, so that no part of the document goes entirely unexamined.
C) The opening and closing sections, since these are what most attendees will actually read before the meeting.
D) The few facts the recommendation depends on, since the decision changes if any one of them turns out to be wrong.
correct_answers: D) The few facts the recommendation depends on, since the decision changes if any one of them turns out to be wrong.
explanations: Confidence of expression is unrelated to whether a claim is load-bearing, and a quietly stated figure can be the one the recommendation turns on.
Even sampling spreads scarce attention across material of very unequal importance, so a decisive figure gets the same scrutiny as background.
Checking what will be read protects the meeting's impression of the document but leaves the reasoning behind the recommendation unexamined.

Correct. With limited time, verification should follow consequence. Identifying the handful of facts that would reverse the recommendation concentrates the check where an error would actually change the outcome.
